prompt: In what sense are the DORA metrics symptoms?

choices.text: They only appear when something is wrong
choices.why: They are measured all the time, good months and bad.

choices.text: They show habits that cannot be seen directly
choices.why: Right. How a team builds and ships is invisible; the four numbers are what it leaves behind.

choices.text: They measure the health of the people on the team
choices.why: They cannot see the people at all; that is one of their blind spots.

choices.text: They are caused by incidents
choices.why: Only two of the four involve failures at all.

prompt: If the Billing team had been told in June to deploy every day, without changing anything else, what would most likely have happened?

choices.text: Every metric would have improved as it did in August
choices.why: August's improvement came from the review queue emptying, which a deploy order does not touch.

choices.text: The team would have shipped more features
choices.why: Features were held up in review, not in the pipeline.

choices.text: The failure rate would have risen sharply
choices.why: Nothing suggests that; daily runs would mostly have carried nothing.

choices.text: Deployment frequency would rise on paper and little else would change
choices.why: Right. The pipeline would run daily and carry whatever the review queue let through, as before.

prompt: Which jobs does the lesson say the DORA metrics are good for? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Noticing that something has changed
choices.why: Right. Before anybody has an opinion about it.

choices.text: Confirming that a change in habits worked
choices.why: Right. As the Billing team's did.

choices.text: Setting each developer's yearly goals
choices.why: They describe a team's system, not a person; lesson 8.

choices.text: Starting a conversation about why
choices.why: Right. The conversation is where the work is.

prompt: Match each capability to its family.

pairs.left: teams able to deploy without asking other teams
failure leads to inquiry, not blame

prompt: The Billing team's August change belongs to which family of capabilities?

choices.text: Process and flow
choices.why: Right. A work-in-progress limit and a review rule; no tooling changed.

choices.text: Technical, because the pipeline started running daily
choices.why: The pipeline's schedule followed the change; the change was how work was held.

choices.text: Architecture, because services were split
choices.why: No services were split.

choices.text: Culture, because the team stopped blaming each other
choices.why: Nothing in the history is about blame.

prompt: A team has a build server and calls it continuous integration, but its branches live for two weeks. What does it have?

choices.text: The capability, since the tool is installed
choices.why: A capability is a habit; the habit here is integrating rarely.

choices.text: A more advanced form of continuous integration
choices.why: Two-week branches are the opposite of integrating continuously.

choices.text: The tool, without the capability
choices.why: Right. A capability is measured by what happens to a change, not by what is installed.

choices.text: Nothing measurable at all
choices.why: Branch age is easy to measure, and here it says a lot.

prompt: A team's time to restore is long. Where does the lesson suggest looking first?

choices.text: At how many story points each sprint delivers
choices.why: Points say nothing about recovery.

choices.text: At monitoring and how easy rollback is
choices.why: Right. Each symptom narrows the search; this one points at detection and undoing.

choices.text: At the length of the backlog
choices.why: The backlog affects lead time from request, not recovery.

choices.text: At the number of people on the team
choices.why: Headcount is not where recovery time usually goes.

prompt: Order Westrum's three kinds of culture from worst to best for how information flows.
Which question can the four DORA metrics not answer?

choices.text: How often do we deploy?
choices.why: That is deployment frequency.

choices.text: How often do our deployments fail?
choices.why: That is change failure rate.

choices.text: How long does a commit take to reach production?
choices.why: That is lead time for changes.

choices.text: Was the change worth making?
choices.why: Right. Value is a product question, measured by outcomes, not deployments.

prompt: In September a Billing requester waited 32.5 days on average, 27.3 of them in the backlog, while DORA's lead time for changes was about 6 hours. How many of the 32.5 days could DORA's lead time see at most, to one decimal place?
Why can a team ship a slow decline in quality while its change failure rate stays at zero?

choices.text: Bugs that never cause a rollback are not change failures
choices.why: Right. The rate counts deployments needing remediation, not every annoyance.

choices.text: Because the rate is only computed once a year
choices.why: It is computed as often as you like.

choices.text: Because small teams cannot have failures
choices.why: The Billing team had four.

choices.text: Because zero is the target every team reaches
choices.why: Zero is neither a target nor typical.

prompt: Two teams show the same improvement in all four metrics. One changed how it works; the other had two people working every weekend. How does a DORA dashboard tell them apart?

choices.text: The weekend team has a higher deployment frequency on Saturdays
choices.why: It may not deploy at weekends at all; the work can land on Monday.

choices.text: The weekend team's change failure rate is always higher
choices.why: Nothing makes that certain; tired people can still ship safely for a while.

choices.text: It does not
choices.why: Right. The four cannot see the people; pair them with a survey and the on-call load.

choices.text: By its time to restore, which shows tiredness
choices.why: Restore time measures recovery, not the people doing it.

prompt: Match each blind spot to a measurement that sees into it.

pairs.right: an outcome chosen before the change shipped
lead time from request to production

prompt: A web team deploys fifteen times a day; the tablet app team releases every two weeks through the app stores. What does that comparison say?

choices.text: That the web team is a hundred times better
choices.why: The number is mostly a property of what each ships.

choices.text: Almost nothing about either team's quality
choices.why: Right. App store review sets the tablet team's pace, whatever its habits.

choices.text: That the tablet team should deploy daily
choices.why: That would be asking the app stores to change.

choices.text: That their definitions of deployment agree
choices.why: Different systems usually mean different definitions too.

prompt: Why does ranking teams by their DORA numbers make the numbers themselves worse as information?

choices.text: Because rankings are published once a year
choices.why: Frequency of publishing is not the problem.

choices.text: Because the best teams stop measuring
choices.why: They keep measuring; what changes is what the measurement answers.

choices.text: Because ranks cannot be computed from medians
choices.why: Anything can be ranked; the problem is behaviour.

choices.text: Teams start optimising how they look
choices.why: Right. Splitting deployments and moving definitions improve the rank, not the team; lesson 7.

prompt: Which comparison of DORA numbers does the lesson call fair?

choices.text: A team against its own past
choices.why: Right. Same system, same definitions, and a known change in between.

choices.text: A team against the industry's elite cluster
choices.why: Those are other organisations' systems and definitions.

choices.text: Two teams in the same company with different products
choices.why: Different products make most of the difference.

choices.text: Each developer against the team's average
choices.why: The metrics are not individual; lesson 8.

prompt: Across a company, DORA numbers are best used to find teams worth talking to, as questions rather than ___.
What is wrong with setting next quarter's targets at eight deployments a week and a failure rate under 3%?

choices.text: The numbers are too low to be ambitious
choices.why: Ambition is not the issue.

choices.text: Targets must be set on lead time first
choices.why: No metric is a better target than another.

choices.text: It turns symptoms into targets without knowing the cause
choices.why: Right. Nobody asked what produced the improvement or what pushing further would cost.

choices.text: Failure rates cannot go below 5%
choices.why: They can; the problem is making them the goal.

prompt: Why does the second reader ask whether the improvement is in the numbers or in the definitions?

choices.text: Because definitions always change each quarter
choices.why: They should not; that is the point of writing them down.

choices.text: A changed definition looks like an improvement
choices.why: Right. Here the definitions held, so the improvement is real.

choices.text: Because DORA forbids changing definitions
choices.why: No such rule; the risk is silent change.

choices.text: Because the definitions decide the team's rank
choices.why: There is no rank in this reading.

prompt: The Billing team's median time to restore went from 166 minutes to 52. By what factor did it fall, to one decimal place?
A platform team deploys twice a month and other teams say it has made them much faster. What should its DORA numbers be taken to mean?

choices.text: That it is a low performer and should be reorganised
choices.why: Its work does not show up as its own deployments.

choices.text: That the other teams are wrong about it
choices.why: Their faster delivery is evidence too.

choices.text: That it should deploy daily to catch up
choices.why: Deploying more would not change what it is for.

choices.text: Little; its value lands in others' work
choices.why: Right. Work that is not a deployment is a blind spot of all four.

prompt: Which line should every DORA dashboard carry beside its four numbers?

choices.text: What the numbers cannot see
choices.why: Right. A good reader spends more time on a dashboard's edges than on its numbers.

choices.text: The team's position in the company ranking
choices.why: Ranking is what the lesson warns against.

choices.text: Next quarter's targets for each metric
choices.why: Targets on symptoms are the first reading's mistake.

choices.text: The names of whoever caused each failure
choices.why: Blame is the opposite of the culture the research found works.
